ev.isl_h_abbasids.title: The black banners
ev.isl_h_abbasids.text: Troops under the black banners of the Abbasids have entered Damascus. Caliph Marwan has fled, and the Umayyad family is being hunted throughout the land. The capital is moving east, to Iraq.
ev.isl_h_abbasids.note: In 750 the Abbasid Revolution overthrew the Umayyad dynasty. Damascus ceased to be the caliphate's capital; almost the entire Umayyad family was wiped out, except Abd al-Rahman, who escaped to Spain.
ev.isl_h_round_city.title: The Round City
ev.isl_h_round_city.text: Caliph al-Mansur is building a new capital on the Tigris - Madinat al-Salam, the "City of Peace": three rings of walls, four gates, and a palace with a green dome at the centre. There is work for everyone - and now there is a spare coin in your household too.
ev.isl_h_round_city.note: Baghdad was founded by Caliph al-Mansur in 762; tens of thousands of workers built the Round City over about four years. Baghdad soon became one of the largest cities in the world.
ev.isl_h_harun.title: Harun al-Rashid
ev.isl_h_harun.text: The young Harun al-Rashid has become caliph, and the viziers of the Barmakid family run the affairs of state. Baghdad grows rich: Chinese silk in the bazaars, poets and musicians in the streets, legends about the caliph's generosity.
ev.isl_h_harun.note: Harun al-Rashid reigned from 786 to 809. His era became Baghdad's "golden age" and later found its way into the tales of the Thousand and One Nights.
ev.isl_h_barmakids.title: The fall of the Barmakids
ev.isl_h_barmakids.text: In a single night Harun ordered the vizier Jafar the Barmakid executed and his family thrown into prison. Their palaces were confiscated. The city whispers: if this can happen to the Barmakids, what about ordinary people?
ev.isl_h_barmakids.note: The sudden fall of the Barmakids in 803 has never been fully explained; court chroniclers offered many different reasons.
ev.isl_h_siege_baghdad.title: The war of the brothers
ev.isl_h_siege_baghdad.text: Harun's sons, al-Amin and al-Ma'mun, could not share the caliphate. Al-Ma'mun's troops are besieging Baghdad; catapults pound the quarters and hungry bands of the poor fight in the streets.
ev.isl_h_siege_baghdad.stay.success: You lived through the siege, though it frightened you badly.
ev.isl_h_siege_baghdad.stay.failure: Your quarter burned, and you were hurt by falling debris.
ev.isl_h_siege_baghdad.note: The civil war of 811–813 ended with a long siege of Baghdad and the death of Caliph al-Amin. His brother al-Ma'mun won.
ev.isl_h_house_wisdom.title: The House of Wisdom
ev.isl_h_house_wisdom.text: Under Caliph al-Ma'mun translators - Christians, Jews, Persians and Arabs - render Aristotle, Galen, Euclid and Indian books on numbers into Arabic. New numerals with a zero have come from India. Scholars give lessons to anyone who wishes.
ev.isl_h_house_wisdom.note: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad was a library and translation centre. Al-Khwarizmi, whose name gave us the word "algorithm", worked there, as did the translator Hunayn ibn Ishaq.
ev.isl_h_mihna.title: The Mihna
ev.isl_h_mihna.text: The caliph demands that judges and scholars affirm that the Qur'an was created. Those who refuse are interrogated, and the famous Ahmad ibn Hanbal is flogged, yet he does not yield. Now they are asking you.
ev.isl_h_mihna.refuse.success: They let you go - too minor a figure. But at the mosque people are proud of you.
ev.isl_h_mihna.refuse.failure: You were flogged and jailed for a month. You did not give in.
ev.isl_h_mihna.note: The Mihna ("trial", 833–848) was the attempt by the caliphs al-Ma'mun, al-Mu'tasim and al-Wathiq to impose the doctrine of the created Qur'an. Al-Mutawakkil ended it; Ibn Hanbal's steadfastness made him a hero.
ev.isl_h_samarra.title: The court leaves for Samarra
ev.isl_h_samarra.text: Caliph al-Mu'tasim and his Turkish guard have left Baghdad up the Tigris and are building a new capital, Samarra. Baghdad is offended: the palaces stand empty, orders have dried up.
ev.isl_h_samarra.note: In 836 the caliphs' residence moved to Samarra because of clashes between the Turkish guard and the people of Baghdad; the court returned to Baghdad in 892.
ev.isl_h_zanj.title: The Zanj rebellion
ev.isl_h_zanj.text: In the south, in the salt marshes near Basra, the Zanj have risen - Black slaves who scraped salt flats to make farmland. They have taken Basra and their boats roam the canals. Baghdad sends army after army.
ev.isl_h_zanj.fear: Pray that the trouble doesn't reach here
ev.isl_h_zanj.join.success: You reached the marshes and vanished. When the rising was crushed, you were already living free under another name.
ev.isl_h_zanj.join.failure: You were caught on the road and returned to your master.
ev.isl_h_zanj.note: The Zanj rebellion (869–883) was one of the largest slave revolts in history. Under Ali ibn Muhammad the rebels sacked Basra in 871; the regent al-Muwaffaq crushed the revolt.
ev.isl_h_buyids.title: The Buyids in Baghdad
ev.isl_h_buyids.text: Persian Daylamite warriors of the Buyid family have entered Baghdad. The caliph keeps his throne, but now he merely signs what the new masters - Shiite emirs - tell him to.
ev.isl_h_buyids.note: In 945 the Buyids seized Baghdad; the Abbasid caliphs kept their religious authority but lost real power.
ev.isl_h_seljuks.title: Tughril Beg
ev.isl_h_seljuks.text: The Seljuk Turk Tughril Beg has ridden into Baghdad, and the caliph has proclaimed him sultan - "the power". Steppe horsemen in the streets, new taxes, but also an order not seen for a long time.
ev.isl_h_seljuks.note: In 1055 the Seljuk Tughril Beg took Baghdad and ended Buyid rule. The Seljuk sultans governed in the name of the Abbasid caliphs.
ev.isl_h_nizamiyya.title: The Nizamiyya
ev.isl_h_nizamiyya.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk has opened a madrasa in Baghdad: students live at the school, get bread and a stipend, and are taught by the finest theologians. They say even the poor will be admitted if they are able.
ev.isl_h_nizamiyya.note: The Nizamiyya madrasa opened in Baghdad in 1067; the great theologian al-Ghazali taught there. A network of such schools trained judges and officials for the Seljuk state.
ev.isl_h_futuwwa.title: The futuwwa brotherhood
ev.isl_h_futuwwa.text: Caliph al-Nasir himself joined the futuwwa brotherhood and made it honourable: the "young men" swear generosity, loyalty and protection of the weak, with special trousers and a cup of salt water at the initiation.
ev.isl_h_futuwwa.note: Caliph al-Nasir (1180–1225) sought to revive the caliphate's power and reorganised the urban futuwwa brotherhoods, joining one himself.
ev.isl_h_mongols.title: The Mongols
ev.isl_h_mongols.text: Khan Hulagu's army has surrounded Baghdad. The walls are breached by catapults, Caliph al-Musta'sim has come out to surrender. The city is given over to plunder. Smoke hangs over the river, and the water, they say, has turned black with the ink of drowned books.
ev.isl_h_mongols.hide.success: You survived. When you came out, your quarter was gone.
ev.isl_h_mongols.hide.failure: They found you. You stayed alive by a miracle.
ev.isl_h_mongols.flee.success: You managed to escape the city. Everything you owned stayed behind.
ev.isl_h_mongols.flee.failure: Horsemen caught the fugitives at the crossing.
ev.isl_h_mongols.note: In February 1258 Hulagu's Mongols took Baghdad; estimates of the dead range from tens to hundreds of thousands, and the caliph was executed. The Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad came to an end. The city survived but was never the same again.
ev.isl_h_emirate.title: The fugitive from Damascus
ev.isl_h_emirate.text: Young Abd al-Rahman, the sole survivor of the Umayyad family, crossed the sea, defeated the governor and proclaimed himself emir of Córdoba. Baghdad is now a foreign power to al-Andalus.
ev.isl_h_emirate.note: In 756 Abd al-Rahman I founded an independent Umayyad emirate in Córdoba.
ev.isl_h_mezquita.title: The Great Mosque
ev.isl_h_mezquita.text: The emir has bought the site of an old church from the Christians and begun building the Great Mosque. Columns are hauled from Roman ruins, and craftsmen set double arches of red brick and white stone on top of them.
ev.isl_h_mezquita.note: Construction of the Great Mosque of Córdoba began around 785 under Abd al-Rahman I; it was enlarged over the next two centuries.
ev.isl_h_caliphate_cordoba.title: The Caliph of Córdoba
ev.isl_h_caliphate_cordoba.text: Abd al-Rahman III has declared himself caliph - Commander of the Faithful, the equal of Baghdad's. Outside the city they are building the palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra, which needs thousands of hands.
ev.isl_h_caliphate_cordoba.note: In 929 Abd al-Rahman III proclaimed the Caliphate of Córdoba; construction of Madinat al-Zahra began in 936. Córdoba became the largest city in Western Europe.
ev.isl_h_fitna.title: The Fitna
ev.isl_h_fitna.text: Caliphs replace one another in quick succession, while Berber bands and mercenaries plunder the suburbs. Madinat al-Zahra has been sacked. Córdoba, the foremost city of the West, is burning from within.
ev.isl_h_fitna.flee: Leave for kin in the countryside
ev.isl_h_fitna.note: The Fitna of al-Andalus (1009–1031) was a civil war in which Córdoba and Madinat al-Zahra were sacked in 1010–1013. In 1031 the caliphate broke up into small "taifa" kingdoms.
ev.isl_h_toledo.title: Toledo has fallen
ev.isl_h_toledo.text: King Alfonso of Castile has taken Toledo, the ancient city at the heart of the peninsula. Terrified, the taifa rulers call for help from the Almoravids - stern Berbers from across the sea.
ev.isl_h_toledo.note: In 1085 Alfonso VI of Castile took Toledo. In 1086 the Almoravids under Yusuf ibn Tashfin landed in Spain and defeated him at Sagrajas (al-Zallaqa).
ev.isl_h_almohads.title: The Almohads
ev.isl_h_almohads.text: Córdoba has been taken by the Almohads, preachers of strict monotheism from Morocco. Christians and Jews are ordered to accept Islam or leave. Many families are loading their belongings onto mules.
ev.isl_h_almohads.note: The Almohads took Córdoba around 1148 and demanded that Jews and Christians convert. The family of the philosopher and physician Maimonides, a native of Córdoba, fled and eventually settled in Fustat (Cairo).
ev.isl_h_cordoba_falls.title: Castilians in Córdoba
ev.isl_h_cordoba_falls.text: King Ferdinand of Castile has taken Córdoba. A cross has been raised over the minaret of the Great Mosque, and Muslims are given time to leave. Those who stay will live under the king.
ev.isl_h_cordoba_falls.note: On 29 June 1236 Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba; the Great Mosque was consecrated as a cathedral. Most Muslims left the city.
ev.isl_h_fatimid_cairo.title: Al-Qahira
ev.isl_h_fatimid_cairo.text: The general Jawhar has led the Fatimid army from Ifriqiya and laid out a new palace-city beside old Fustat: al-Qahira, "the Victorious". Palaces, walls and the al-Azhar mosque are going up; the whole quarter finds work.
ev.isl_h_fatimid_cairo.note: The Fatimids were an Ismaili dynasty that proclaimed its own caliphate in North Africa. In 969 they took Egypt and founded Cairo; the al-Azhar mosque opened in 972.
ev.isl_h_hakim.title: The whims of al-Hakim
ev.isl_h_hakim.text: Caliph al-Hakim issues decree after decree: banning the eating of mulukhiyya, women going out in the street, trading at night. Christians are ordered to wear heavy crosses, churches are being closed, and in Jerusalem, they say, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre has been destroyed.
ev.isl_h_hakim.note: The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim (996–1021) was known for strange prohibitions and persecutions of Christians and Jews in 1009–1013, including the destruction of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009. He later reversed many decrees.
ev.isl_h_shidda.title: The Great Calamity
ev.isl_h_shidda.text: For several years running the Nile has failed to flood properly, while the troops fight over power and plunder. Bread costs as much as silver. They say even the caliph is selling palace treasures to feed his household.
ev.isl_h_shidda.hoard: Save every handful for your own
ev.isl_h_shidda.note: The "Great Calamity" (al-shidda al-uzma) of 1065–1072 was a time of famine and turmoil in Fatimid Egypt; order was restored by the vizier Badr al-Jamali.
ev.isl_h_saladin_cairo.title: The end of the Fatimids
ev.isl_h_saladin_cairo.text: In the Friday sermon the name of the Baghdad caliph was spoken instead of the Fatimid one. The last Fatimid is dying, and power now lies with the Kurd Salah al-Din - Saladin.
ev.isl_h_saladin_cairo.note: In 1171 Saladin abolished the Fatimid caliphate and founded the Ayyubid dynasty; he also began building the Citadel of Cairo.
ev.isl_h_mansura.title: Crusaders at Mansura
ev.isl_h_mansura.text: The French king Louis has landed at Damietta and is marching on Cairo. The sultan is dying, but his Mamluks have trapped the Franks in the alleys of Mansura. The city is gathering men and grain for the army.
ev.isl_h_mansura.enlist.success: The Franks were beaten and King Louis taken prisoner. You came home a hero.
ev.isl_h_mansura.enlist.failure: You were wounded in the very first clash.
ev.isl_h_mansura.note: The Seventh Crusade (1248–1254): Louis IX took Damietta in 1249 but was defeated at Mansura in 1250 and captured. The victory strengthened the Mamluks, who soon seized power.
ev.isl_h_mamluks.title: The sultana and the Mamluks
ev.isl_h_mamluks.text: The Mamluks killed the last Ayyubid, and Shajar al-Durr - the late sultan's widow, a former slave - took the throne. A few months later she married the Mamluk emir Aybak. The country is ruled by slave-soldiers.
ev.isl_h_mamluks.note: In 1250 the Mamluk Sultanate arose in Egypt - a state whose ruling elite were warriors bought as children and later freed. It lasted until 1517.
ev.isl_h_qalawun.title: Qalawun's hospital
ev.isl_h_qalawun.text: Sultan Qalawun has built a huge hospital: it treats everyone - rich and poor, Muslim and Christian, men and women - free of charge. It has a pharmacy, a kitchen and a lecture hall for physicians.
ev.isl_h_qalawun.note: Sultan Qalawun's bimaristan in Cairo opened in 1285 and ran for centuries; it had wards for different illnesses and musicians to soothe the patients.
ev.isl_h_cairo_crisis.title: Famine and copper money
ev.isl_h_cairo_crisis.text: The Nile failed, then came plague and dearth. Silver has vanished from the markets, everything is bought with copper, and prices jump every day. The streets are full of people begging for bread.
ev.isl_h_cairo_crisis.note: The crisis of 1403–1406 in Mamluk Egypt was described in detail by the historian al-Maqrizi, who blamed the debasement of coinage and official abuses.
ev.isl_h_ottoman_cairo.title: The Ottomans in Cairo
ev.isl_h_ottoman_cairo.text: Sultan Selim's army, with its cannon and Janissaries, has crushed the Mamluks. The last sultan, Tumanbay, was hanged at the Bab Zuwayla gate. Egypt is now a province ruled from Istanbul.
ev.isl_h_ottoman_cairo.note: In 1516–1517 Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq and Raydaniyya and took Cairo. The Ottomans carried many craftsmen off to Istanbul, along with the last Abbasid caliph.
ev.isl_h_damascus_feud.title: The tribal feud
ev.isl_h_damascus_feud.text: The old feud between the "northern" and "southern" Arab tribes has flared again: they say a stolen melon started the bloodshed. The quarters of Damascus are barricaded, and houses burn at night.
ev.isl_h_damascus_feud.note: In the 790s Damascus and its surroundings were torn by a bloody feud between the Qaysi and Yemeni tribes; Harun al-Rashid sent troops to end it.
ev.isl_h_fatimid_damascus.title: The Fatimids in Damascus
ev.isl_h_fatimid_damascus.text: The army of the Cairo caliph has taken Damascus. The mosques now name the Fatimid caliph and use Shiite formulas, while the Sunni townsfolk grumble and wait for change.
ev.isl_h_fatimid_damascus.note: In 970 the Fatimids took Damascus; their hold on the city was shaky and often contested.
ev.isl_h_first_crusade.title: Jerusalem has fallen
ev.isl_h_first_crusade.text: Franks with crosses on their cloaks have taken Jerusalem and slaughtered its people. Refugees walk the roads - no belongings, empty eyes. The qadi of Damascus weeps in the mosque, but the rulers are busy with their own quarrels.
ev.isl_h_first_crusade.note: The First Crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099; the massacre of its people shocked the Muslim world, but the rulers of Syria and Egypt were slow to unite.
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.title: The siege of Damascus
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.text: The kings of France and Germany, with the Franks of Jerusalem, have reached Damascus and camped in the orchards of the Ghouta. The townsfolk fight for every wall among the fruit trees.
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.fight.success: After four days the Franks withdrew. The Second Crusade had failed at the walls of Damascus.
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.fight.failure: An arrow wounded you in an orchard by a canal.
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.supply: Carry water and bread to the defenders
ev.isl_h_damascus_1148.note: The siege of Damascus in July 1148 lasted four days and ended with the Crusaders' retreat - the failure of the Second Crusade.
ev.isl_h_nur_din.title: Nur al-Din
ev.isl_h_nur_din.text: Nur al-Din, ruler of Aleppo, has taken Damascus without much bloodshed. He builds madrasas, a hospital and bathhouses, abolishes illegal levies and calls for a holy war against the Franks.
ev.isl_h_nur_din.note: Nur al-Din Zengi united Syria by taking Damascus in 1154; his hospital, the Nuri bimaristan, served Damascus for centuries.
ev.isl_h_hattin.title: Hattin and Jerusalem
ev.isl_h_hattin.text: Saladin has crushed the Franks at the Horns of Hattin, in waterless heat, and in autumn he entered Jerusalem. Unlike the Franks ninety years before, he let the townspeople go for ransom. The mosques are full of thanksgiving.
ev.isl_h_hattin.enlist.success: You were at Hattin and at the walls of Jerusalem, and came back with spoils.
ev.isl_h_hattin.enlist.failure: A Frankish sword caught you in the final charge.
ev.isl_h_hattin.note: On 4 July 1187 Saladin destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem at Hattin, and on 2 October he took Jerusalem.
ev.isl_h_ain_jalut.title: Ain Jalut
ev.isl_h_ain_jalut.text: In spring the Mongols entered Damascus, and it seemed nothing could stop them. But at the spring of Ain Jalut in Galilee the Mamluks of Qutuz and Baybars routed the Mongol army. Damascus is free again, and Baybars will soon be sultan himself.
ev.isl_h_ain_jalut.wary: Wait and see what comes next
ev.isl_h_ain_jalut.note: On 3 September 1260 the Mamluks defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut - one of the first major Mongol defeats. Qutuz was soon assassinated, and Baybars became sultan.
ev.isl_h_black_death.title: The Black Death
ev.isl_h_black_death.text: The plague has come. Every day hundreds of biers are carried out of the gates, and the gravediggers cannot keep up. The whole city gathers to pray - Muslims, Christians and Jews together.
ev.isl_h_black_death.pray.success: The plague moved on, and you are still alive.
ev.isl_h_black_death.pray.failure: The sickness came for you after all.
ev.isl_h_black_death.flee: Go out into the desert, away from people
ev.isl_h_black_death.flee.success: You waited out the plague far from the city.
ev.isl_h_black_death.note: The Black Death of 1347–1349 killed perhaps a third of the people of Egypt and Syria. The historian Ibn al-Wardi, who described the plague in Syria, himself died of it in 1349.
ev.isl_h_timur.title: Timur
ev.isl_h_timur.text: Timur's army stands before Damascus. The Mamluk sultan has gone back to Cairo, the townsfolk surrendered hoping for mercy, but the city was squeezed for ransom and then set ablaze. The craftsmen - armourers, glassblowers, weavers - are being driven off to Samarkand.
ev.isl_h_timur.hide.failure: They found you. You barely survived.
ev.isl_h_timur.flee.success: You got out of the city while it burned.
ev.isl_h_timur.note: Timur took Damascus in 1401; the city was plundered and burned, and the Great Mosque badly damaged. The historian Ibn Khaldun, who was in the city, met Timur. Many craftsmen were deported to Samarkand.
ev.isl_h_ottoman_damascus.title: Marj Dabiq
ev.isl_h_ottoman_damascus.text: Near Aleppo the Ottoman cannon shattered the Mamluk army, and the old sultan al-Ghawri fell. A month later Damascus opened its gates to Sultan Selim without a fight.
ev.isl_h_ottoman_damascus.note: On 24 August 1516 Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq; Syria, including Damascus, became part of the Ottoman Empire.
ev.isl_h_repopulate.title: New citizens
ev.isl_h_repopulate.text: After the siege the city is half empty, and Sultan Mehmed is repopulating it: Muslims, Greeks, Armenians and Jews are brought from Anatolia and the Balkans, empty houses are handed out, mosques, baths and markets are built.
ev.isl_h_repopulate.note: After taking Constantinople in 1453, Mehmed II carried out forced resettlements (sürgün) to the capital; by 1477 the city had about 80,000 people, roughly 60% of them Muslims.
ev.isl_h_topkapi.title: The new palace
ev.isl_h_topkapi.text: On the point above the Bosphorus the sultan is building a new palace - Topkapı: courtyards, gardens, pavilions, a treasury, kitchens for thousands. Masons, carpenters and tile-makers are needed.
ev.isl_h_topkapi.look: Gawk at the building from a boat
ev.isl_h_topkapi.note: Topkapı Palace was built in 1459–1478 and served as the residence of the Ottoman sultans for almost four centuries.
ev.isl_h_quake_1509.title: The Lesser Judgement Day
ev.isl_h_quake_1509.text: The earth lurched so hard that hundreds of houses and part of the city walls collapsed, and waves surged across the Sea of Marmara. For weeks people live in tents in the gardens, afraid to go back under roofs.
ev.isl_h_quake_1509.dig.success: You pulled a neighbour out from under the stones, and he swears eternal friendship.
ev.isl_h_quake_1509.dig.failure: A wall collapsed and pinned you.
ev.isl_h_quake_1509.note: The earthquake of 10 September 1509 in Istanbul, known as the "Lesser Judgement Day", destroyed thousands of houses; Bayezid II mustered tens of thousands of workers to rebuild the walls.
ev.isl_h_suleiman.title: Süleyman
ev.isl_h_suleiman.text: Sultan Selim has died, and his son Süleyman has taken the throne - young, tall, a lover of poetry and order. He ordered abusive officials punished and let the craftsmen deported from Egypt go home. The city expects a great reign.
ev.isl_h_suleiman.note: Süleyman I (1520–1566) was the longest-reigning Ottoman sultan. Europe called him the Magnificent; his own people called him Kanuni, "the Lawgiver".
ev.isl_h_mohacs.title: The Hungarian campaign
ev.isl_h_mohacs.text: The sultan is leading his army west: on Belgrade, on Hungary, and they say on Vienna. Soldiers, carters, armourers and biscuit bakers are needed. Istanbul hums like a stirred-up hive.
ev.isl_h_mohacs.march.success: After Mohács you came home with plunder and stories of the Hungarian plains.
ev.isl_h_mohacs.march.failure: Before Vienna it rained, the wagons bogged down, and fever laid you low.
ev.isl_h_mohacs.note: In 1526 Süleyman defeated the Hungarians at Mohács; in 1529 he besieged Vienna but withdrew because of the weather and overstretched supply lines.
ev.isl_h_suleymaniye.title: The Süleymaniye
ev.isl_h_suleymaniye.text: On the third hill the architect Sinan is raising Sultan Süleyman's mosque: a dome, four minarets, madrasas, a hospital, a soup kitchen for the poor, baths. They say the mortar is mixed with egg white and that Sinan knows every mason by name.
ev.isl_h_suleymaniye.pray: Go to the first Friday prayer
ev.isl_h_suleymaniye.note: The Süleymaniye complex was built by Mimar Sinan in 1550–1557. Sinan, himself a product of the devshirme, designed hundreds of buildings over his long life.
ev.isl_h_coffee_istanbul.title: The first coffeehouses
ev.isl_h_coffee_istanbul.text: Two Syrians, Hakem from Aleppo and Şems from Damascus, have opened shops in the Tahtakale quarter where coffee is brewed. Poets, out-of-office judges, teachers and idlers gather there - playing backgammon and chess and talking late into the night. The imams complain that the mosques are emptying.
ev.isl_h_coffee_istanbul.note: According to the historian Peçevi, the first coffeehouses in Istanbul opened in 1554–1555. In the 16th-17th centuries the authorities tried to ban them more than once, without success.
ev.isl_h_suleiman_death.title: The death of Süleyman
ev.isl_h_suleiman_death.text: The old sultan died on campaign before the Hungarian fortress of Szigetvár. The vizier hid his death from the army until the heir Selim arrived. Istanbul is in mourning: for almost half a century he was the only sultan people could remember.
ev.isl_h_suleiman_death.note: Süleyman died on 6 or 7 September 1566 during the siege of Szigetvár; the grand vizier Sokollu Mehmed kept his death secret for several weeks.
ev.isl_h_lepanto.title: After Lepanto
ev.isl_h_lepanto.text: At Lepanto the allied Christian fleet destroyed almost the entire Ottoman navy. But the shipyards on the Golden Horn work day and night, and over a single winter more than a hundred new galleys are launched. "You shaved our beard, but we cut off your arm," the vizier tells the Venetians, recalling Cyprus.
ev.isl_h_lepanto.note: The Battle of Lepanto on 7 October 1571 was a heavy defeat for the Ottoman fleet; yet by 1572 the fleet had been rebuilt, and Cyprus, taken in 1571, stayed Ottoman.
ev.isl_h_observatory.title: The observatory torn down
ev.isl_h_observatory.text: Taqi al-Din's observatory on the Tophane hill has been torn down by the sultan's order: the chief mufti said that prying into the heavens brings misfortune, and the wars and plague of recent years prove it.
ev.isl_h_observatory.note: Taqi al-Din's Istanbul observatory operated from 1577 to 1580 and was demolished in January 1580.
